position_in_era.historical_role: Heir to the self-titled template: the riff is built on a detuned, slow-moving power chord sequence whose pace and weight directly inherit the self-titled's tempo-as-gravity approach. Iommi's guitar runs through a ring modulator, giving it the metallic 'iron' timbre that names the song. The first Black Sabbath song in which the riff's sonic texture (robot-voice quality) is the narrative itself.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded June 1970, Regent Sound / Island Studios, London. Iommi fed his guitar through a ring modulator to achieve the robotic tonality — the riff's texture tells the story of a man turned to iron. Tempo is deliberately ponderous: approx. 75 bpm, slower than almost any preceding rock song. Produced by Rodger Bain.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: The riff is so dominant that Osbourne's vocal fits into its gaps rather than leading the song. Butler's bass follows Iommi's guitar line rather than establishing an independent counter-melody. Ward's drumming is minimal and lockstep — the riff is the only protagonist.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Iommi: Gibson SG through a ring modulator and Laney amplifier; Butler: Fender Precision Bass (C# tuning); Ward: Ludwig kit; Osbourne: vocal. The ring modulator was borrowed from a session musician — Iommi has cited its use as accidental and unrepeatable in exactly that form.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Released on the Paranoid album September 1970. The song became one of Sabbath's most recognised live pieces and a touchstone for detuned, slow-riff composition. Ranked by Rolling Stone as one of the greatest guitar riffs in rock history.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Paranoid album recorded and mixed in two days at Island Studios. Iron Man's three-minute riff-loop structure proved that minimal repetition and maximum weight could be commercially viable — it reached the UK top 40 as a single in 1971.
